title: 11th Grade Language Arts — English III
subtitle: Advanced Universal 36-Week College, Career & Civic Literacy Course

units.title: Advanced Foundations of Reading, Writing & Language
units.essential: How do advanced readers and writers establish accurate, ethical, and independent habits of inquiry?
units.summary: Establish diagnostic baselines, disciplined close reading, evidence-based interpretation, paraphrase, etymology, syntax, revision, academic integrity, and college-ready study habits.
units.assessment: Advanced diagnostic portfolio: annotated literary and informational texts, analytical response, language revision, source-use check, and growth plan.

units.title: Literary Layers, Style & Universal Themes
units.essential: How do form, style, culture, and historical context shape enduring human questions?
units.summary: Evaluate literary elements, diction, syntax, voice, figurative language, and universal themes through globally diverse short fiction, essays, and literary nonfiction.
units.assessment: Comparative literary analysis evaluating style and universal theme across texts from different periods or cultures.

units.title: Perspective, Juxtaposition & Literary Argument
units.essential: How do authors position readers to evaluate character, perspective, mood, and meaning?
units.summary: Analyze juxtaposition, perspective, mood, symbolism, and literary reasoning; develop a polished evidence-based literary argument and oral defense.
units.assessment: Publication-ready literary analysis essay, oral defense, revision memo, and unit portfolio.

units.title: Classical Rhetoric, Structure & Persuasion
units.essential: How do speakers and writers construct authority, logic, urgency, and audience response?
units.summary: Study classical rhetoric alongside comparative global traditions; evaluate text structure, purpose, rhetorical situations, appeals, and the ethical use of persuasion.
units.assessment: Rhetorical situation dossier and timed analysis of a complex speech or essay.

units.title: Comparative Argument & Civic Discourse
units.essential: How should informed people evaluate competing claims, evidence, assumptions, and consequences?
units.summary: Compare multiple arguments on shared issues; detect fallacies and bias; evaluate evidence, reasoning, counterclaims, and contemporaneous perspectives across civic, scientific, historical, and cultural texts.
units.assessment: Source-based argument evaluation, deliberative seminar, and evidence-based civic argument.

units.title: Rhetorical Composition & Midyear Mastery
units.essential: How do writers transform analysis, evidence, and audience awareness into consequential communication?
units.summary: Compose rhetorical analysis, refine oral argument, synthesize first-semester learning, complete a cumulative midterm, and build an evidence-based improvement plan.
units.assessment: Rhetorical analysis essay, oral presentation, cumulative midterm, corrections, and midyear conference.

units.title: Poetry Across Periods, Places & Traditions
units.essential: How do poets use compressed language to address the pressures of their time and place?
units.summary: Analyze poetry from ancient, classical, medieval, Renaissance, Indigenous, African, Asian, Middle Eastern, European, Caribbean, and American traditions with attention to form, speaker, sound, imagery, context, and translation.
units.assessment: Comparative poetry notebook, unseen-poem analysis, and contextual interpretation.

units.title: Comparative Poetry, Performance & Digital Interpretation
units.essential: How do comparison, performance, translation, and medium change the meaning of a poem?
units.summary: Compare contemporaneous poets and translated works; compose sustained poetry analysis; perform and create ethical multimedia interpretations for authentic audiences.
units.assessment: Comparative poetry essay, oral interpretation, and accessible multimedia adaptation.

units.title: Literary Research, Source Evaluation & Synthesis
units.essential: How do researchers build trustworthy knowledge from primary, secondary, quantitative, and multimedia evidence?
units.summary: Develop research questions, refine scope, evaluate authority and bias, distinguish primary and secondary evidence, cite ethically, and synthesize sources without flattening disagreement.
units.assessment: Research proposal, annotated bibliography, source credibility audit, synthesis matrix, and conference.

units.title: Research Writing, Narrative Craft & Publication
units.essential: How can writers organize complex knowledge and experience for different audiences and media?
units.summary: Write a sustained researched analysis, an expository synthesis, and a complex narrative; integrate graphics and multimedia; revise for accessibility, precision, coherence, and publication ethics.
units.assessment: Multi-source research paper, complex narrative, digital presentation, publication checklist, and author reflection.

units.title: Drama, Performance & Long-Form Reading
units.essential: How do dramatic form, performance choices, and sustained reading reveal conflict and human motive?
units.summary: Study drama through stagecraft, rhetoric, juxtaposition, performance, and interpretation; launch a long-form novel or narrative nonfiction study using independent reading plans and seminar protocols.
units.assessment: Drama analysis/performance and long-form reading dossier with annotations, motif tracking, and conference.

units.title: Global Synthesis, Portfolio & Final Examination
units.essential: What evidence demonstrates readiness for senior-level, college, career, and civic literacy?
units.summary: Complete the long-form study, compare global themes and author choices, curate a standards-based portfolio, lead a conference, complete a cumulative final, and create a senior-readiness plan.
units.assessment: Long-form comparative analysis, final portfolio, student-led conference, cumulative final examination, corrections, and readiness plan.

quiz.question: In a fictional account, a mayor calls a new school proof of 'unanimous civic progress.' A petition written before the opening asks for lower fees and safer roads. Which conclusion best evaluates both sources?
choices: The petition proves that no one welcomed the school.
The speech confirms that every family could attend.
The school opening and unresolved access barriers could both be true.
The speech proves its author deliberately hid the petition.
quiz.explanation: The documents may describe a real achievement and also reveal unmet access needs; neither excerpt establishes the mayor's intent.

quiz.question: An archive displays a September letter next to a note signed by an editor twenty years later. Which attribution is best supported?
choices: Describe the editor's note as a later interpretation distinct from the letter.
Quote the editor's note as a statement by the original letter writer.
Treat both passages as one eyewitness account of September.
Ignore the date difference because the passages share a page.
quiz.explanation: The letter and later editor's note have different authors and dates, so their statements must be attributed separately.

quiz.question: Which action best demonstrates mastery of Week 01: Course Launch: English III Scholar Habits?
choices: Choose a conclusion before reading the sources
Focus on formatting while ignoring reasoning
Rely on summary without testing evidence
read closely, reason from evidence, communicate clearly, revise purposefully, and reflect on mastery
quiz.explanation: This week requires students to read closely, reason from evidence, communicate clearly, revise purposefully, and reflect on mastery.

quiz.question: English III · Week 01 (Course Launch: English III Scholar Habits): Original paired sources: An official statement calls a new library “a success.” Visitor logs show high use downtown but substantially lower use from two outlying neighborhoods. A city official calls the new library 'a success,' while visitor logs show uneven neighborhood access. Which conclusion is supported?
choices: The opening was achieved, but the evidence leaves the reach of its benefits unresolved.
The official intentionally concealed every visit count.
The library served nobody because access was uneven.
The logs prove that every neighborhood agreed about the opening.
quiz.explanation: Distinguish an institution's action from access and intentions that require more evidence.

quiz.question: English III · Week 01 (Course Launch: English III Scholar Habits): Which thesis qualifies its inference from the conflicting documents?
choices: 'The speech, the logs demonstrates, unequal benefit.'
'Because the logs, the speech should be ignored.'
'The speech celebrates the opening, while the logs raise questions about who benefited.'
'The speech proves no readers benefited at all.'
quiz.explanation: A qualified comparison separates the documents' different evidentiary claims.

quiz.question: Two witnesses describe a meeting: one recalls applause, while another recalls silence after a challenging question. What is the strongest annotation?
choices: The witnesses are both unreliable and should be excluded.
The audience certainly fell silent before the applause.
The difference proves that one witness intentionally lied.
The accounts may refer to different moments; a recording could clarify sequence.
quiz.explanation: Without a shared timeline, the responses could have occurred at different moments, so independent evidence is needed to determine sequence.

quiz.question: A fictional source states: 'The committee delayed publication because supporting evidence was incomplete.' Which paraphrase conveys the meaning accurately?
choices: The committee published promptly despite incomplete evidence.
Missing supporting information led the committee to postpone release.
The committee concealed complete evidence to delay publication.
A shortage of members prevented the scheduled release.
quiz.explanation: The committee postponed publication because of incomplete evidence; the other options reverse, invent, or alter the stated cause.

quiz.question: Which action best demonstrates mastery of Week 02: Close Reading, Inference, and Paraphrase?
choices: Focus on formatting while ignoring reasoning

read closely, reason from evidence, communicate clearly, revise purposefully, and reflect on mastery
Choose a conclusion before reading the sources
quiz.explanation: This week requires students to read closely, reason from evidence, communicate clearly, revise purposefully, and reflect on mastery.

quiz.question: English III · Week 02 (Close Reading, Inference, and Paraphrase): A paragraph quotes a witness's vivid language but does not consider the witness's vantage point. What is the analytical gap?
choices: Every witness at the same event must agree.
The account's reliability and limits have not been evaluated.
The witness's wording is too dramatic to cite.
The quotation's spelling makes the source inaccurate.
quiz.explanation: An inference depends on what the witness could observe and how testimony is framed.

quiz.question: English III · Week 02 (Close Reading, Inference, and Paraphrase): Which sentence differentiates observation from inference?
choices: 'The pause proves the speaker was dishonest.'
'The witness reports, therefore all attendees hesitated.'
'The witness, a pause indicates it occurred.'
'The witness reports a pause; that silence may indicate hesitation.'
quiz.explanation: Reports and tentative interpretation should be attributed separately.

quiz.question: In 'The report qualified its conclusion because records were missing,' what does 'qualified' mean?
choices: Missing records automatically invalidated every finding.
The report's author had gained a professional license.
The conclusion was limited by the evidence available.
The report established which archives were accredited.
quiz.explanation: Here qualified means narrowed or made conditional; the missing records limit the supported scope of the conclusion.

quiz.question: A draft says, 'The witness described an empty square the footage showed a crowd.' Which revision correctly separates independent clauses and preserves the contrast?
choices: The witness described an empty square, the footage showed a crowd.
The witness described an empty square because the footage showed a crowd.
The witness described an empty square although, the footage showed a crowd.
The witness described an empty square; the footage showed a crowd.

A character’s name
A chapter number

Only using the title
Ignoring changes

Only liking the speech
Only counting paragraphs

Rely on summary without testing evidence

quiz.question: English III · Week 12 (Rhetorical Appeals: Logos, Ethos, Pathos, Kairos): A speaker cites shared experience before giving statistics. Which appeal does that opening primarily develop?
choices: Proof that the statistics are exact.
A complete causal explanation.
A legal obligation to agree.
Credibility and identification with the audience.
quiz.explanation: An appeal to common experience can help build ethos without independently validating data.

quiz.question: English III · Week 12 (Rhetorical Appeals: Logos, Ethos, Pathos, Kairos): Which sentence identifies both device and likely effect?
choices: 'The speaker shares experience because the audience is unanimous.'
'The personal account establishes a shared frame before numerical evidence appears.'
'The statistics appear, therefore the story is false.'
'The speaker's experience equals statistical proof.'
quiz.explanation: The observation connects sequence with audience reception without treating it as proof.

monday.misconception: Do not let preview work become summary only. The learner should connect context, vocabulary, and source conditions to the essential question: How can sources support but not replace original interpretation?
monday.evidence: Preserve a context/vocabulary record that shows how at least two terms or source details change the learner’s initial understanding.

tuesday.model: Model one evidence chain from Research notes from multiple sources Include primary, secondary, quantitative, visual, and multimedia sources with diverse scholarly viewpoints.: precise observation → accurate paraphrase or quotation → inference → reasoning → significance. tuesday.misconception: Annotation is not evidence by itself. Require an explanation of why the selected detail matters and what alternative reading or limitation remains.
tuesday.evidence: Preserve one ranked evidence set with a strongest detail, a weaker detail, and a written justification for the ranking.

wednesday.model: Model a small section of Synthesis note cards and integrated paragraph. Make the reasoning visible: controlling idea, evidence choice, commentary, organization, and the language focus (paraphrase, synthesis, quotation integration, signal phrases, and source relationships).

wednesday.evidence: Preserve a plan plus a substantive draft excerpt that demonstrates the week’s language focus and one self-identified revision target.

thursday.model: Model feedback on Synthesis note cards and integrated paragraph using the actual success criteria for Synthesis and Source Integration: represent the writer’s idea fairly, test evidence and reasoning, then recommend one precise revision.
thursday.misconception: Feedback should not be preference-based (“I like it”). Require comments tied to evidence, reasoning, audience, accuracy, or paraphrase, synthesis, quotation integration, signal phrases, and source relationships.
thursday.evidence: Preserve one peer/teacher feedback record and a revision memo explaining what changed, why it changed, and what effect the revision should have.

friday.model: Retrieve the week’s core ideas without rereading first, then transfer them to a fresh example before completing the mastery check. Revisit the essential question: How can sources support but not replace original interpretation?

quiz.question: Before collecting sources for Research-supported literary analysis draft, what is the strongest first research move?
choices: A random source list
A copied essay
A yes/no answer only
A focused interpretive question about a text or author
quiz.explanation: Research should serve interpretation.

quiz.question: A learner needs a primary source for Literary Analysis with Research. Which option belongs in that category?
choices: Only ads
The literary text itself, letters, speeches, journals, or original documents
Only student comments
Only encyclopedia summaries
quiz.explanation: Primary sources come from the period or original creator.

quiz.question: Which action best demonstrates mastery of Week 28: Literary Analysis with Research?
choices: form a focused inquiry, evaluate source quality, integrate evidence ethically, and explain relationships among sources
Choose a conclusion before reading the sources
Focus on formatting while ignoring reasoning
Rely on summary without testing evidence
quiz.explanation: This week requires students to form a focused inquiry, evaluate source quality, integrate evidence ethically, and explain relationships among sources.

quiz.question: English III · Week 28 (Literary Analysis with Research): A paper uses a historical lens but cites no passage from the novel. What is needed?
choices: More general historical facts unrelated to the novel.
An argument that context always determines meaning.
A title with more theoretical vocabulary.
Direct textual evidence demonstrating how the relevant historical feature operates in the work.
quiz.explanation: Literary research integrates historical framing with analyzed text.

quiz.question: English III · Week 28 (Literary Analysis with Research): Which thesis remains open to competing interpretations?
choices: 'The author's private wishes are certain from this detail.'
'The recurring image of travel evokes opportunity, yet later scenes complicate that promise.'
'The novel proves all travel is liberation.'
'The image always means opportunity in every culture.'
quiz.explanation: Qualification is grounded in development across scenes.

Only one word
Logical reasoning, credible evidence, and elaboration
Only plot summary
quiz.explanation: Grade 11 writing emphasizes researched, elaborated analysis.

quiz.question: Expository analysis should use...
choices: Logical organization and tone/voice appropriate to task and audience
No structure
Only slang
Only questions
quiz.explanation: Organization and tone matter.

quiz.question: English III · Week 29 (Expository Analysis of Complex Texts): An expository essay treats a summary of an article as its own claim. How should the writer distinguish the voices?
choices: Attribute the article's conclusion, then explain how the writer evaluates it.
Rewrite the conclusion as a quotation with no citation.
Delete all analysis because summaries are objective.
Present the source's assumptions as established facts.

'The report attributes the decline to staffing; that explanation requires data from comparable sites.'
'Staffing caused the decline, because the report says so.'
quiz.explanation: A source attribution is followed by a checkable limitation.

lessons.title: Launch, Context & Vocabulary
lessons.objective: Frame Final Review and Final Test and build the cultural, historical, disciplinary, and vocabulary knowledge needed for independent analysis.
lessons.miniLesson: Introduce the essential question: “How can I demonstrate readiness for 12th grade ELA?” Model how an advanced Grade 11 reader previews context, genre, source conditions, audience, and key vocabulary: final, readiness, mastery, reflection, next step.
lessons.guidedPractice: Preview the text/source family: Review packet, portfolio, and selected passages Encourage a global or cross-cultural comparison in the culminating long-form analysis. Complete a notice–wonder–context routine and identify how standards ELA.11.R.2.4, ELA.11.R.3.4, ELA.11.C.1.3 will be demonstrated.
lessons.independentWork: Create an advanced vocabulary and context record, then write an initial 8–10 sentence response to the essential question that includes one qualification or uncertainty.
lessons.evidence: Context notes, vocabulary applications, source preview, and initial interpretation
lessons.support: Use chunked text, audio or text-to-speech, vocabulary supports, guided annotation, sentence frames, reduced visual load, oral rehearsal, extended time, or an equivalent accessible pathway while preserving the same reasoning target.
lessons.extension: Locate a credible comparative text, translation note, historical artifact, or disciplinary source that complicates the week’s central question.

lessons.title: Close Reading, Evidence & Evaluation Lab
lessons.objective: Apply advanced close reading to synthesize course learning, manage timed tasks, explain corrections, and set evidence-based next steps.
lessons.miniLesson: Model a multi-pass reading: comprehension and structure; evidence and author choices; context and assumptions; then evaluation of significance, effectiveness, limitations, and alternative interpretations.
lessons.guidedPractice: Annotate at least ten purposeful details in the assigned source. Classify evidence by standard, rhetorical or literary function, context, and reliability. Apply the language focus: cumulative analysis, timed writing, editing, synthesis, and senior-readiness planning.
lessons.independentWork: Complete an evidence matrix: observation → quotation or data → paraphrase → inference → reasoning → significance → limitation or counterreading. Rank the evidence and justify the ranking.
lessons.evidence: Annotated source, evidence matrix, defensible interpretation, and limitation/counterreading
lessons.support: Use chunked text, audio or text-to-speech, vocabulary supports, guided annotation, sentence frames, reduced visual load, oral rehearsal, extended time, or an equivalent accessible pathway while preserving the same reasoning target.
lessons.extension: Develop and test a plausible counterinterpretation, alternate line of reasoning, or competing explanation using different evidence.

lessons.title: Advanced Composition & Craft Studio
lessons.objective: Transform reading, research, and discussion into the week’s major product: Cumulative final examination, corrections analysis, portfolio reflection, and senior-readiness plan.
lessons.miniLesson: Analyze a mentor text for thesis or controlling idea, line of reasoning, organization, integrated evidence, commentary, style, audience, and cumulative analysis, timed writing, editing, synthesis, and senior-readiness planning.
lessons.guidedPractice: Plan the product with a rhetorical situation or interpretive problem, a nuanced claim, evidence sequence, reasoning notes, counterpoint, and audience/purpose check. Draft one demanding section through modeling or collaborative rehearsal.
lessons.independentWork: Draft the major product: Cumulative final examination, corrections analysis, portfolio reflection, and senior-readiness plan. Highlight the strongest synthesis or evaluation, identify one gap in evidence or reasoning, and note one ethical or accessibility consideration.
lessons.evidence: Plan, substantive draft, evidence integration, and self-identified revision targets
lessons.support: Use chunked text, audio or text-to-speech, vocabulary supports, guided annotation, sentence frames, reduced visual load, oral rehearsal, extended time, or an equivalent accessible pathway while preserving the same reasoning target.
lessons.extension: Recast a section for a substantially different audience, medium, culture, or disciplinary context and explain the consequences of each change.

lessons.title: Seminar, Feedback & Substantive Revision
lessons.objective: Use collaborative inquiry and revision to improve intellectual fairness, precision, coherence, evidence, style, and audience impact.
lessons.miniLesson: Practice advanced feedback: represent the writer’s claim accurately, identify a strength, test assumptions and evidence, ask a genuine question, identify a reasoning gap, and recommend a precise revision.
lessons.guidedPractice: Conduct a seminar or conference around “How can I demonstrate readiness for 12th grade ELA?” Use multiple pieces of evidence, paraphrase another perspective fairly, and distinguish disagreement about evidence, reasoning, values, or definitions.
lessons.independentWork: Revise the Wednesday product substantially. Complete a revision memo documenting at least four meaningful changes, the evidence or feedback that prompted them, and the effect on the reader, listener, or viewer.
lessons.evidence: Seminar record, feedback, revised product, source/ethics check, and revision memo
lessons.support: Use chunked text, audio or text-to-speech, vocabulary supports, guided annotation, sentence frames, reduced visual load, oral rehearsal, extended time, or an equivalent accessible pathway while preserving the same reasoning target.
lessons.extension: Respond to the strongest counterargument or counterinterpretation and state what evidence could legitimately change your conclusion.

lessons.title: Mastery Check, Corrections & Portfolio
lessons.objective: Demonstrate weekly mastery, complete error analysis, preserve evidence, and determine whether to advance or repeat targeted practice.
lessons.miniLesson: Review standards language, vocabulary, and a common misconception. Model correction as a reasoning process: identify the tested skill, diagnose the error, cite the governing evidence or rule, and show the corrected reasoning.
lessons.guidedPractice: Complete retrieval practice and a short transfer task using an unfamiliar passage, source, or scenario. Identify one priority before the quiz.
lessons.independentWork: Take the weekly quiz. Complete corrections for missed items. File the strongest artifact and process evidence in the portfolio. Write a 4–6 sentence reflection connecting mastery evidence to the essential question and the next goal.
lessons.evidence: Quiz score, corrections, transfer task, portfolio artifact, and reflection
lessons.support: Use chunked text, audio or text-to-speech, vocabulary supports, guided annotation, sentence frames, reduced visual load, oral rehearsal, extended time, or an equivalent accessible pathway while preserving the same reasoning target.
lessons.extension: Create one rigorous original question with four plausible choices, one definitive answer, an explanation, and the standard or skill assessed.
